theme: The Word made flesh; the first disciples, “come and see”
readingInstruction: Read John 1:1-51. John begins before creation, with the Word, then moves to John the Baptist, the first disciples, and Nathanael. Read verses 1-18 slowly, as the prologue to the whole Gospel.
settingTheScene: John was one of the Twelve, the disciple whom Jesus loved, and he wrote this Gospel late in his life. He tells us his purpose near the end: that we may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name. His Gospel is different from Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It contains very little of the parables and much more of Jesus’ long conversations, and it is built around seven signs and seven “I AM” statements. It begins with a hymn that takes us back to the beginning of everything.
observation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (1:1).
“The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (1:5).
“But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (1:12).
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (1:14).
“No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (1:18).
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (1:29).
“Philip said to him, Come and see” (1:46).
“You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (1:51).
interpretation:
The Gospel opens with the words of Genesis 1:1, “In the beginning.” But now the focus is not on creation but on the one through whom it came. The Word was with God (distinct from the Father) and the Word was God (fully divine). He was in the beginning, so he is eternal. “All things were made through him,” so he is Creator. In him was life, and that life was the light of men.

Then John says that the light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it. He introduces John the Baptist, a witness who points to the light. The true light came into the world, yet the world did not know him, and his own people did not receive him. But to those who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God, born not of blood or the will of the flesh but of God. That promise is the core of the Gospel.

Verse 14 is the center of the prologue: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” The word for dwelt means pitched his tent, an echo of the tabernacle in the wilderness. God has come to live with his people in a person. “We have seen his glory,” says John, “full of grace and truth,” which recalls the LORD’s self-revelation to Moses in Exodus 34. The law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has seen God, but the Son has made him known.

The rest of the chapter is a parade of titles. John the Baptist points to Jesus: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” Andrew finds Peter, saying, “We have found the Messiah.” Philip finds Nathanael, who doubts that anything good could come from Nazareth, and Philip answers with an invitation: “Come and see.” Jesus tells Nathanael that he saw him under the fig tree, and Nathanael confesses, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus promises he will see greater things: heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man, an echo of Jacob’s ladder at Bethel. Jesus himself is the meeting place between heaven and earth.
connection: Genesis 1:1-3 is the beginning John echoes. Proverbs 8:22-31 speaks of wisdom beside God at creation. Exodus 25:8 and 33:18-23 are about God dwelling with his people and showing his glory. Exodus 34:6 is the source of “grace and truth.” Isaiah 53:7 is the Lamb. Genesis 28:12 is Jacob’s ladder. Hebrews 1:1-3 states that the Son is the radiance of the glory of God. 1 John 1:1-4 is John’s own testimony to what he saw and touched.
application:
Read John 1:1-18 aloud three times. Which phrase strikes you most? Write it down.

Take Philip’s invitation, “Come and see,” and ask yourself who you could invite to see Jesus.

Praise Jesus today as Creator, as the light in darkness, and as the Lamb who takes away sin.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for becoming flesh and making his dwelling among us.
Tell him, “I’ll come and see,” and ask him to show you more.
Ask him to give you the right to be his child.
